title: Arthritis Medication: What Works and What to Expect
meta_title: Arthritis Medication: UK Treatment and Safety Guide
meta_description: Understand arthritis medicines, NICE advice for osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, monitoring, side effects and NHS prescription costs across the UK.
excerpt: How medicines for osteoarthritis and inflammatory arthritis differ, what NICE recommends, and what to ask about safety, monitoring and NHS costs.

content:
Quick answer: Arthritis treatment depends on the diagnosis. For knee osteoarthritis, NICE recommends a topical NSAID if medicine is needed; paracetamol and opioids are not routine treatments. Inflammatory arthritis may need disease-modifying medicines to control disease activity. Your clinician should agree the benefits, risks, monitoring and review plan with you.

Which arthritis medicine is right for which condition?

There is no single medication ladder for every type of arthritis. Medicines used to ease osteoarthritis pain are different from medicines used to control rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Pain relief does not replace disease-modifying treatment when that is needed.

This is a general guide for adults in the UK, not a prescription or a complete list of treatments and side effects. Use the leaflet supplied with your medicine and your own clinician's plan. Do not start, change or stop prescribed treatment on the basis of this page. Tell your pharmacist or prescriber about all medicines, supplements, allergies, health conditions and any pregnancy plans.

NSAIDs: gels, tablets and safety

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen, reduce pain and inflammation. For osteoarthritis, NICE NG226 says medicines should support non-drug treatment, including therapeutic exercise, and be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time.

  • Knee osteoarthritis: offer a topical NSAID, such as a suitable gel applied to the skin.
  • Osteoarthritis in other joints: consider a topical NSAID.
  • If topical treatment is unsuitable or ineffective: consider an oral NSAID after assessing stomach, kidney, liver and cardiovascular risks, other medicines and individual circumstances.

For oral NSAID treatment in osteoarthritis, NICE recommends offering a stomach-protecting medicine, such as a proton pump inhibitor (PPI). NICE also recommends a PPI with oral NSAIDs used for RA symptoms. A PPI does not remove all NSAID risks.

Some ibuprofen tablets and topical products can be bought without a prescription. Oral naproxen, oral diclofenac and COX-2 inhibitors such as celecoxib are prescription medicines. Availability depends on the particular product. COX-2 medicines are not risk-free alternatives: the same careful safety assessment is needed.

NSAIDs can cause stomach ulcers or bleeding, kidney problems, allergic reactions and cardiovascular problems. Topical products generally have fewer side effects than tablets, but still need to be suitable for you. Ask a pharmacist or doctor first if you have a history of ulcers, heart or kidney disease, asthma, are pregnant, or take other medicines. Do not combine different NSAIDs, or add an over-the-counter NSAID to prescribed treatment, without professional advice. This is particularly important if you take methotrexate, blood thinners or steroids.

Paracetamol and opioids are not routine osteoarthritis treatment

Paracetamol

It is misleading to call paracetamol the routine first medicine for osteoarthritis. NICE says there is no strong evidence of benefit. Do not routinely offer paracetamol or weak opioids for osteoarthritis unless they are used infrequently for short-term relief and all other drug treatments are unsuitable, not tolerated or ineffective.

If paracetamol is appropriate for your circumstances, follow the packet and your clinician's advice. The right dose can differ, for example if you weigh under 50 kg or have liver problems. Do not take it with another product containing paracetamol, including some cold remedies and combination painkillers such as co-codamol. NHS advice is not to use it for more than 3 days unless a doctor tells you to.

Codeine and other opioids

NICE says do not offer strong opioids for osteoarthritis because their risks outweigh the benefits. Severe pain is a reason to review the diagnosis and treatment plan, not an automatic reason to progress to morphine or another strong opioid.

Opioids can cause constipation, nausea, sleepiness, dependence and addiction. Prolonged use can lead to dependence even at prescribed doses, and overdose can be fatal. If an opioid is prescribed for another appropriate reason, agree what benefit is expected, when it will be reviewed and how treatment will end. Do not drive if it makes you sleepy. Do not stop long-term opioids suddenly: ask your prescriber for a gradual reduction plan.

DMARDs for rheumatoid arthritis

Disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) control inflammatory disease activity rather than simply relieving pain. They are not a treatment for osteoarthritis. Treatment choices for other inflammatory arthritides depend on the specific diagnosis; RA recommendations should not be copied to every condition.

For newly diagnosed active RA, NICE NG100 recommends first-line conventional DMARD treatment with oral methotrexate, leflunomide or sulfasalazine as soon as possible, ideally within 3 months of persistent symptoms starting. That is not an instruction to wait. Hydroxychloroquine can be considered for mild or palindromic disease. Treatment is adjusted towards remission or low disease activity, with additional medicines if needed.

  • Methotrexate for inflammatory arthritis is taken once a week, not every day. Follow the exact day and dose on your prescription. Taking it daily by mistake or taking more than prescribed needs urgent medical advice, even if you feel well.
  • Onset varies: DMARDs are not immediate painkillers. Benefit may build over weeks or months, depending on the medicine and the person. Do not use a single 6-to-12-week deadline for every drug.
  • Monitoring varies: methotrexate needs blood tests, especially when starting or changing treatment. Hydroxychloroquine has different checks, including eye monitoring where indicated. Ask for the schedule for your actual medicine, rather than assuming every DMARD has the same blood-test plan.

Some treatments increase infection risk. Your rheumatology team should explain which symptoms to report, vaccination advice and what to do if you become unwell. Get prompt advice about possible infection or troublesome side effects rather than waiting for your next routine appointment. Do not make a blanket decision to skip or stop every medicine: follow the advice for your drug and situation.

Biologics and targeted treatments

Biological DMARDs, such as adalimumab or etanercept, target parts of the inflammatory process and are given by injection or infusion. Targeted synthetic DMARDs, including JAK inhibitors, are a separate group; they are not biologics.

Eligibility depends on the medicine, diagnosis, disease activity, previous treatments and safety assessment. It is not correct to say biologics are only for high-activity RA. NICE includes some options for moderate RA (DAS28 3.2 to 5.1) after an inadequate response to intensive therapy with at least two conventional DMARDs used in combination. Other options have different criteria. Your specialist should explain the applicable pathway.

Screening and ongoing monitoring are needed. JAK inhibitors carry MHRA warnings about serious infections, blood clots, cardiovascular events and cancer. In people aged 65 or over, current or past long-term smokers, and those with certain cardiovascular or cancer risk factors, they should only be used when no suitable alternatives are available. Your specialist should discuss individual risks and alternatives.

Steroid tablets and injections

Corticosteroids reduce inflammation. In RA, short-term treatment may be used while a new DMARD takes effect or for a flare. Long-term steroids are not a routine substitute for effective disease control: NICE limits continuing long-term RA treatment to situations where complications have been discussed and other treatment options offered.

For osteoarthritis, NICE says a joint corticosteroid injection may be considered when other drug treatments are ineffective or unsuitable, or to support exercise. Explain that relief is short term, 2 to 10 weeks, rather than promising months of benefit. The number and spacing of injections depend on the joint, product, response and risks; there is no universal allowance of three or four injections per joint each year.

Risks depend on dose, route and duration. They can include infections, raised blood sugar, mood changes and, with longer-term treatment, osteoporosis and high blood pressure. Do not stop steroid treatment without speaking to your prescriber. Some courses need gradual dose reduction. Ask whether you need a steroid alert or emergency card and what to do if you become ill.

NHS access and prescription costs

Your GP, pharmacist and specialist team can explain who prescribes, supplies and monitors each medicine. Specialist treatment does not always follow the same supply route as a routine GP prescription.

Checked on 25 November 2026, the standard NHS prescription charge in England is £9.90 per item for people who pay. Exemptions and help with costs may apply. An NHS Prescription Prepayment Certificate costs £32.05 for 3 months or £114.50 for 12 months and may save money if you pay for regular prescriptions. Check the current NHS prices and eligibility before buying.

Do not apply England's charge across the UK. NHS prescriptions are generally free in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, but cross-border issue and dispensing rules can affect charges. Ask your pharmacist or check NHSBSA's cross-border guidance. Ask a pharmacist about suitable and affordable over-the-counter options; do not stockpile painkillers or buy extra to change your treatment yourself.

What to agree with your clinician

  • What is my diagnosis, and is this medicine for symptoms or disease control?
  • What improvement should I expect, and when will we review it?
  • What tests, eye checks or other monitoring do I need, and who arranges them?
  • What should I do about missed doses, infection, pregnancy plans or side effects?
  • Who do I contact between appointments, and what is the stopping or reduction plan?

Bring an up-to-date list of prescribed medicines, shop-bought medicines and supplements. Record how symptoms affect sleep, walking and daily tasks, rather than changing doses yourself.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 for an immediate emergency: severe breathing difficulty, sudden swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, collapse or inability to wake someone. A very unwell person with confusion, very fast breathing or blue, pale or blotchy skin may have sepsis and needs emergency help. Do not wait for a routine medicine review.

Get urgent medical advice now if you have taken more paracetamol than the packet allows, or more methotrexate than prescribed, including taking weekly methotrexate daily by mistake, even if you feel well. Call NHS 111 in England, Scotland or Wales. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service for urgent assessment; call 999 in an emergency.

A sudden very painful, hot or swollen joint, or difficulty moving or bearing weight on it, needs urgent assessment, even without a fever. Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact the urgent-care route above. It could be joint infection, not simply an arthritis flare. Also seek urgent advice about suspected serious medicine side effects, including vomiting blood, black stools, new breathlessness or signs of infection while taking immune-suppressing treatment. Call 999 if symptoms are severe or life-threatening.
